analysis.one_liner: Requires ranked choice voting for all congressional elections, with federal money to help states run it.
analysis.headline: A bill to require ranked choice voting in every Senate and House election was introduced with zero cosponsors in September 2024, was referred to the Senate Rules Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require every state to use ranked choice voting for Senate and House elections starting in 2027, letting voters rank up to five candidates instead of picking just one. It would ban separate runoff elections, spell out exactly how ballots are counted in rounds, and pay states $4 to $8 per registered voter for new equipment, software, poll worker training, and voter education. Voters and the Attorney General could sue states that don't comply, with fast-track review in federal courts.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters gain the ability to rank candidates rather than choose one, so they can support a favorite without worrying their vote helps the candidate they like least; winners would emerge from head-to-head comparisons rather than a divided field. Third-party and independent candidates benefit because voting for them no longer risks "wasting" a vote or acting as a spoiler. States with separate runoff elections, which draw low turnout and add cost, would no longer hold them. State election offices receive federal payments sized to their number of registered voters to cover the switch.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, third-party candidates, and state election offices

how_it_helps.text: Voters could rank up to five candidates in every Senate and House election, primary, special, and general, instead of being forced to pick a single candidate, so supporting a long-shot or third-party candidate no longer risks helping a voter's least-preferred candidate win.
The bill bans separate runoff elections for congressional seats, ending low-turnout second rounds in states that use them; the ranked-choice count itself settles which candidate wins.

The bill sets a uniform national counting method: the lowest vote-getter is eliminated round by round and those ballots transfer to the voter's next choice, with specific rules for skipped rankings, ties, and exhausted ballots.

States would receive a federal payment of $4 to $8 per registered voter, specifically to cover voting equipment updates, software licenses, ballot printing, poll worker training, audits and recounts, and voter education about the new system.

The bill is enforceable: any person in a state could sue over a failure to comply, the Attorney General could act, and courts must expedite the case and hear it on a fast schedule tied to the election calendar.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the state payments, which the bill authorizes at 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dollar cap; applied to the nation's roughly 215 million registered voters, the $4-to-$8-per-voter formula works out to somewhere between about $850 million and $1.7 billion. State election offices do the real work: reprogramming machines, redesigning ballots, retraining poll workers, and educating voters, though the federal payment is meant to cover those costs. States that currently use runoff elections lose that option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and state election offices

drawbacks.text: It is a sweeping federal mandate that overrides how all 50 states currently run congressional elections, based on Congress's power to set the 'time, place and manner' of federal elections; that reading invites court challenges and takes choices away from state legislatures and voters who might prefer their current system.

Ranked-choice ballots are more complex: the bill itself contains lengthy rules for skipped rankings, duplicate rankings, exhausted ballots, and ties, and ties would be broken by lot, meaning a race could turn on a random draw.

Round-by-round tabulation is slower than a single count, which can delay election results by days and add strain to audit and recount procedures the bill acknowledges by requiring payments to cover them.
The funding authorization is open-ended ('such sums as may be necessary'), so the actual federal cost depends entirely on future appropriations rather than a fixed budget line.

The enforcement design funnels every lawsuit through a three-judge federal court and direct appeal to the D.C. Circuit sitting en banc, a fast but unusual track that concentrates election litigation in one court and bars damage awards to winning plaintiffs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change is genuinely pro-voter: ranking candidates removes the spoiler problem and the low-turnout runoff, and the bill pays states rather than merely ordering them around. But the costs are real and the design is aggressive: an unfunded-mandate risk is mostly covered by the per-voter payment, yet the federal government dictating a single voting method to every state, ties broken by lot, slower result reporting, and an open-ended appropriation are fair objections an honest supporter would have to concede. Whether the voter-choice gains outweigh the complexity depends heavily on how well states execute the transition.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, referred to the Rules Committee, and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the bill on September 12, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress, with no cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration, the committee with jurisdiction over federal election law.
The committee took no further action: no hearing, no markup, and no vote appear in the bill's action history for the rest of the Congress.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor or the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing election system and the major parties and incumbents it elects: no state had to change how it runs congressional elections, and no senator ever had to vote on the record for or against ranked choice voting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo and incumbent officeholders

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; no senator from either party joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration (chaired by Sen. Amy Klobuchar)
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over federal election law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 12, 2024 and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress: no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: The full Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill after referral; it never reached the floor or received a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the partisan shape is unknown beyond the fact that its only sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.industry: Election technology and voting equipment vendors
industries.note: The bill requires every state to update voting equipment, election software, and ballot design, and pays states $4 to $8 per registered voter expressly to cover equipment, software licenses, programming, and training. That converts the mandate into guaranteed, federally funded demand for vendors, with the public benefit depending on those systems working correctly.

Ranked choice voting removes vote-splitting and spoiler dynamics that can cost a major party seats, and lets states keep party primaries. But it also bans separate runoffs, and any state choosing a nonpartisan blanket primary must advance at least three candidates, weakening the two-candidate head-to-heads that favor established parties.

They must reprogram systems, redesign ballots, retrain poll workers, and educate voters on a new counting method, but the bill funds that transition per registered voter and covers audits, recounts, and reporting.
